claim: During flight maneuvers, insects exhibit compensatory head movements which are essential for stabilizing the visual field on their retina, reducing motion blur, and supporting visual self-motion estimation.
source: During flight maneuvers, insects exhibit compensatory head movements which are essential for stabilizing the visual field on their retina, reducing motion blur, and supporting visual self-motion estimation.
evidence: This is a general statement about insect behavior presented in the abstract without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: In Diptera, compensatory head movements are mediated via visual feedback from their compound eyes that detect retinal slip, as well as rapid mechanosensory feedback from their halteres.
source: In Diptera, such head movements are mediated via visual feedback from their compound eyes that detect retinal slip, as well as rapid mechanosensory feedback from their halteres – the modified hindwings that sense the angular rates of body rotations.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about Dipteran sensory systems.

claim: Halteres are modified hindwings that sense the angular rates of body rotations.
source: halteres – the modified hindwings that sense the angular rates of body rotations.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about halteres based on established knowledge.

claim: Non-Dipteran insects lack halteres.
source: Because non-Dipteran insects lack halteres, it is not known if mechanosensory feedback about body rotations plays any role in their head stabilization response.
evidence: This is a statement of established taxonomic knowledge about insect anatomy.

claim: It is not known if mechanosensory feedback about body rotations plays any role in head stabilization response in non-Dipteran insects.
source: Because non-Dipteran insects lack halteres, it is not known if mechanosensory feedback about body rotations plays any role in their head stabilization response.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: Diverse non-Dipteran insects rely on visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback for flight control.
source: Diverse non-Dipteran insects are known to rely on visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback for flight control.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about non-Dipteran insect sensory systems.

claim: In hawkmoths, reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback severely compromises their ability to control flight.
source: In hawkmoths, for instance, reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback severely compromises their ability to control flight.
evidence: This references prior research findings about hawkmoth flight control.

claim: When the head movements of freely flying moths are restricted, their flight ability is severely impaired.
source: Similarly, when the head movements of freely flying moths are restricted, their flight ability is also severely impaired.
evidence: This statement references prior observations about moth flight.

claim: In the nocturnal hawkmoth Daphnis nerii, compensatory head movements are mediated by combined visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback.
source: Here, we show that in the nocturnal hawkmoth Daphnis nerii, compensatory head movements are mediated by combined visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Head stabilization in moths is mediated primarily by visual feedback during roll movements at lower frequencies.
source: Our study suggests that head stabilization in moths is mediated primarily by visual feedback during roll movements at lower frequencies, whereas antennal mechanosensory feedback is required when roll occurs at higher frequency.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data comparing responses at different frequencies and light conditions.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory feedback is required when roll occurs at higher frequency.
source: Our study suggests that head stabilization in moths is mediated primarily by visual feedback during roll movements at lower frequencies, whereas antennal mechanosensory feedback is required when roll occurs at higher frequency.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data comparing responses at different frequencies with and without antennal feedback.

claim: At adequate light levels, visual feedback is sufficient for head stabilization primarily at low frequencies of body roll.
source: At adequate light levels, visual feedback is sufficient for head stabilization primarily at low frequencies of body roll.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing head stabilization at 2 Hz under twilight conditions.

claim: Under dark conditions, antennal mechanosensory feedback is essential for the control of head movements at high frequencies of body roll.
source: However, under dark conditions, antennal mechanosensory feedback is essential for the control of head movements at high frequencies of body roll.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing impaired head stabilization at 6 Hz in dark conditions when antennae are clipped.

claim: Gaze stabilization is of central importance for reducing motion blur during locomotor behaviors such as flight or walking.
source: For the control of locomotor behaviors such as flight or walking, the ability to stabilize gaze is of central importance for reducing motion blur (Land, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Land, 1999.

claim: Gaze stabilization is achieved through sensorimotor circuits that rapidly sense and correct any deviation from the intended course.
source: In diverse animals, gaze stabilization is achieved through sensorimotor circuits that rapidly sense and correct any deviation from the intended course, typically by eliciting reflexive motor responses of their head and body (Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Land, 1999; Waespe and Henn, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Optomotor reflexes refer to behaviors that occur in response to optic flow.
source: Of these, a class of responses called optomotor reflexes refer to those behaviors that occur in response to optic flow (Borst, 2014).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by a citation.

claim: In most flying animals including insects, birds, and bats, eye movements relative to the head are either reduced or absent.
source: Although gaze stabilization typically requires eye as well as neck movements, in most flying animals including insects (Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Kemppainen et al., 2022; Land, 1999), birds (Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Necker, 2007), and bats (Eitan et al., 2019), eye movements relative to the head are either reduced or absent.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations across different animal groups.

claim: Flying animals with reduced or absent eye movements stabilize their gaze primarily using head and body movements guided by optomotor reflexes.
source: Such animals stabilize their gaze primarily using head and body movements guided by optomotor reflexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about reduced eye movements and general knowledge about gaze stabilization mechanisms.

claim: In insects, optomotor reflexes have mostly been studied in tethered flies (Diptera) using assays in which their heads were fixed to the thorax with glue.
source: In insects, optomotor reflexes have mostly been studied in tethered flies (Diptera) using assays in which their heads were fixed to the thorax with glue while they were presented with a moving display (Borst, 2014).
evidence: This describes established experimental methodology, supported by citation.

claim: Head-fixation adversely affects mechanical power output for flight in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Recent work on the fruit flies Drosophila melanogaster suggests that head-fixation adversely affects mechanical power output for flight (Cellini and Mongeau, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cellini and Mongeau, 2020.

claim: Head-fixation in tethered Drosophila impairs their ability to fixate on specific objects moving relative to ground.
source: Moreover, head-fixation in tethered Drosophila impairs their ability to fixate on specific objects moving relative to ground; if an object is moving relative to a moving ground, wing movements depend on both object and ground motion, but head movements depend only on ground motion (Fox and Frye, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fox and Frye, 2014.

claim: Head-fixation affects steering maneuvers in locusts Locusta migratoria.
source: Head-fixation has also been shown to affect steering maneuvers in locusts Locusta migratoria (Robert and Rowell, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Robert and Rowell, 1992.

claim: Head and wing movements are crucial in steering maneuvers during flight and contribute strongly to gaze stabilization.
source: Head and wing movements are thus crucial in steering maneuvers during flight and contribute strongly to gaze stabilization.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statements about the effects of head-fixation.

claim: In Diptera, head stabilization is mediated by feedback from multiple sensory systems including visual feedback from compound eyes and mechanosensory feedback from halteres.
source: In Diptera, head stabilization is mediated by feedback from multiple sensory systems. These include visual feedback from their compound eyes and the mechanosensory feedback and/or feedforward control from their halteres which are modified hindwings that detect aerial rotations (Hengstenberg, 1988; Hengstenberg, 1993; Schwyn et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mechanosensory proprioceptive structures in the ventral neck-prothorax region called prosternal organs aid in head positioning in Diptera.
source: Additionally, mechanosensory proprioceptive structures in the ventral neck-prothorax region called prosternal organs also aid in head positioning (Paulk and Gilbert, 2006; Preuss and Hengstenberg, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The relative contributions of sensory systems to head stabilization depend on the angular speed of the maneuver because vision typically provides feedback at slower rates than mechanosensors.
source: The relative contributions of these sensory systems depend on the angular speed of the maneuver because vision typically provides feedback at slower rates than mechanosensors (Hengstenberg, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: During aerial maneuvers, haltere feedback combines non-linearly with visual feedback in some neck motor neurons to determine compensatory head movements.
source: Importantly, during aerial maneuvers, haltere feedback combines non-linearly with visual feedback in some neck motor neurons to determine the compensatory head movements (Huston and Krapp, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Huston and Krapp, 2009.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback from halteres is transduced at faster rates than visual feedback.
source: Because mechanosensory feedback from halteres is transduced at faster rates than visual feedback, it is hypothesized to play a key role in guiding wing movements during rapid maneuvers, whereas visual feedback mediates slower turns (Sherman and Dickinson, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Haltere feedback is hypothesized to play a key role in guiding wing movements during rapid maneuvers, whereas visual feedback mediates slower turns.
source: Because mechanosensory feedback from halteres is transduced at faster rates than visual feedback, it is hypothesized to play a key role in guiding wing movements during rapid maneuvers, whereas visual feedback mediates slower turns (Sherman and Dickinson, 2003).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis and supported by a citation.

claim: Rapid head turns precede sharp saccadic turns in freely flying insects.
source: Free-flight studies in diverse insects (honeybees Apis mellifera; Boeddeker and Hemmi, 2010; Wehner and Flatt, 1977, blowflies Calliphora vicina; Hateren and Schilstra, 1999) show that rapid head turns precede sharp saccadic turns, whereas gaze stabilization between saccades ensures that the visual field largely translates over the retina, thereby enabling depth perception.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on honeybees and blowflies.

claim: Gaze stabilization between saccades ensures that the visual field largely translates over the retina, thereby enabling depth perception.
source: Free-flight studies in diverse insects (honeybees Apis mellifera; Boeddeker and Hemmi, 2010; Wehner and Flatt, 1977, blowflies Calliphora vicina; Hateren and Schilstra, 1999) show that rapid head turns precede sharp saccadic turns, whereas gaze stabilization between saccades ensures that the visual field largely translates over the retina, thereby enabling depth perception.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to free-flight studies.

claim: Freely flying bees adjust their head angle based on wide-field image movement in their visual field when flying through a patterned, oscillating drum.
source: When flying through a patterned, oscillating drum surrounding their nest entrance, freely flying bees adjust their head angle based on wide-field image movement in their visual field (Boeddeker and Hemmi, 2010; Wehner and Flatt, 1977).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Visually induced head roll response is limited beyond specific roll frequencies in bees.
source: Moreover, visually induced head roll response is limited beyond specific roll frequencies, suggesting constraints to visually mediated gaze stabilization (Boeddeker and Hemmi, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and suggests an inference about constraints.

claim: Optic flow plays a key role in head stabilization behavior in both tethered and freely flying insects.
source: These studies demonstrate that optic flow plays a key role in head stabilization behavior in both tethered and freely flying insects.
evidence: This is a summary statement drawing on the previously cited studies.

claim: Head stabilization in wasps appears to be primarily visually mediated, although some degree of feedforward control has been suggested.
source: Head stabilization in wasps appears to be primarily visually mediated, although some degree of feedforward control has been suggested (Viollet and Zeil, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Viollet and Zeil, 2013.

claim: In day-flying insects such as dragonflies, head stabilization appears to be dominated by visual feedback.
source: Similarly, in day-flying insects such as dragonflies, head stabilization appears to be dominated by visual feedback, and these insects contain adaptations that ensure passive inertial head stabilization (Gorb, 1999; Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Mittelstaedt, 1950).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dragonflies contain adaptations that ensure passive inertial head stabilization.
source: Similarly, in day-flying insects such as dragonflies, head stabilization appears to be dominated by visual feedback, and these insects contain adaptations that ensure passive inertial head stabilization (Gorb, 1999; Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Mittelstaedt, 1950).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dragonflies achieve precise visual fixation of targets during prey capture in flight.
source: Yet, being predatory insects, they achieve precise visual fixation of targets during prey capture in flight (Lin and Leonardo, 2017; Olberg et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Dragonfly antennae are very small and they do not possess halteres.
source: The role of mechanosensory feedback in head movements in dragonflies remains an open question, especially as their antennae are very small and they do not possess halteres (Gewecke et al., 1974).
evidence: This is a statement of anatomical fact supported by a citation.

claim: Nocturnal ants can stabilize their heads in darkness during walking, suggesting mechanosensory input for stabilization.
source: In contrast, nocturnal ants can stabilize their heads in darkness during walking, suggesting mechanosensory input for stabilization (Raderschall et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and includes an inference about mechanosensory input.

claim: The mechanosensors mediating head stabilization in non-Dipteran insects are yet to be identified.
source: However, the mechanosensors mediating head stabilization in non-Dipteran insects are yet to be identified.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Johnston's organ is a highly sensitive mechanosensory structure situated in the antennal pedicel-flagellar joint of all insects.
source: One potential candidate for the mechanosensory mediation of head stabilization is the Johnston's organ, which is a highly sensitive mechanosensory structure situated in the antennal pedicel-flagellar joint of all insects (e.g. Gewecke, 1974; Sant and Sane, 2018).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: In hawkmoths, the Johnston's organ consists of hundreds of concentrically arranged scolopidial units that are range-fractionated.
source: In hawkmoths, the Johnston's organ consists of hundreds of concentrically arranged scolopidial units that are range-fractionated, which means that the scolopidial units are tuned to different frequency ranges with high sensitivity (Dieudonné et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dieudonné et al., 2014.

claim: Range-fractionated scolopidial units are tuned to different frequency ranges with high sensitivity.
source: In hawkmoths, the Johnston's organ consists of hundreds of concentrically arranged scolopidial units that are range-fractionated, which means that the scolopidial units are tuned to different frequency ranges with high sensitivity (Dieudonné et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definitional explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Antennal mechanosensors contribute in sensing airflow.
source: Antennal mechanosensors contribute in sensing airflow (Roy Khurana and Sane, 2016; Natesan et al., 2019; Taylor and Krapp, 2007), and maintaining headwind orientation (Fuller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Antennal mechanosensors contribute to maintaining headwind orientation.
source: Antennal mechanosensors contribute in sensing airflow (Roy Khurana and Sane, 2016; Natesan et al., 2019; Taylor and Krapp, 2007), and maintaining headwind orientation (Fuller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fuller et al., 2014.

claim: In moths, flight becomes unstable when the mechanosensory load on the Johnston's organ is reduced by clipping off their flagella.
source: In moths, flight becomes unstable when the mechanosensory load on the Johnston's organ is reduced by clipping off their flagella (Dahake et al., 2018; Sane et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In walking crickets, antennae contribute to compensatory head roll.
source: In walking crickets, there is evidence that antennae contribute to compensatory head roll (Horn and Bischof, 1983) and electrophysiological recordings from the neck motor system in flies further revealed that the ventral cervical nerve motor neuron in flies receive input from the antennae (Haag et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Horn and Bischof, 1983.

claim: The ventral cervical nerve motor neuron in flies receives input from the antennae.
source: In walking crickets, there is evidence that antennae contribute to compensatory head roll (Horn and Bischof, 1983) and electrophysiological recordings from the neck motor system in flies further revealed that the ventral cervical nerve motor neuron in flies receive input from the antennae (Haag et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haag et al., 2010.

claim: Under twilight condition at 2 Hz, the compensation error was low with a median ± standard error of mean of 0.4±0.02.
source: Under twilight condition at 2 Hz, the compensation error was low with a median ± standard error of mean of 0.4±0.02 (open circles, Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: When moths were rotated at 2 Hz under dark condition, the compensation error increased to 1.2±0.09.
source: However, when we rotated the moths at 2 Hz under dark condition (filled circles, Figure 2A and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C), a reduction in gain (twilight condition median: 0.6, dark condition median: 0.4) and a shift in phase (twilight condition circular median: 177.6°, dark condition circular median: 302.4°, Figure 3—figure supplement 3: Cases 1 and 2) increased the compensation error to 1.2±0.09, suggesting a severe reduction in their ability to generate compensatory head movements (p=0.0078, Supplementary file 1c, 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments with statistical significance, supported by data in figures.

claim: At 2 Hz under dark conditions, there is a severe reduction in moths' ability to generate compensatory head movements.
source: However, when we rotated the moths at 2 Hz under dark condition (filled circles, Figure 2A and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C), a reduction in gain (twilight condition median: 0.6, dark condition median: 0.4) and a shift in phase (twilight condition circular median: 177.6°, dark condition circular median: 302.4°, Figure 3—figure supplement 3: Cases 1 and 2) increased the compensation error to 1.2±0.09, suggesting a severe reduction in their ability to generate compensatory head movements (p=0.0078, Supplementary file 1c, 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing increased compensation error.

claim: Visual input plays a crucial role in mediating head stabilization at 2 Hz.
source: Thus, visual input plays a crucial role in mediating head stabilization at 2 Hz (Video 1).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of twilight and dark conditions at 2 Hz.

claim: At 6 Hz under twilight condition, the compensation error was 0.7±0.02.
source: We next increased the oscillation frequency to 6 Hz, and observed that under the twilight condition, the compensation error was 0.7±0.02 (open circles, Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments, supported by data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: At 6 Hz, the compensation error remained largely unaltered between twilight and dark conditions with a median ± standard error of mean of 0.7±0.05 (p=0.5469).
source: The compensation error (Figure 2C) remained largely unaltered with a median ± standard error of mean of 0.7±0.05 (p=0.5469, Supplementary file 1c, 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical test showing no significant difference.

claim: At 6 Hz, severe reduction of visual feedback did not greatly hamper head stabilization, suggesting that an additional mechanosensory feedback played a role.
source: Thus, at 6 Hz, severe reduction of visual feedback did not greatly hamper head stabilization, suggesting that at roll rotation of higher frequency, an additional – perhaps mechanosensory – feedback played a role in head stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing maintained head stabilization at 6 Hz in dark conditions.

claim: At 2 Hz, the compensation error was significantly different between the flagella-intact and flagella-clipped groups under both twilight and dark conditions.
source: Under both twilight and dark conditions at 2 Hz (Figure 3E), the compensation error was significantly different between the flagella-intact (twilight: 0.4±0.02; dark: 1.2±0.09) and flagella-clipped groups (twilight: 0.5±0.01; dark: 1±0.01, p=0.0107, p=0.0133, Supplementary file 1c, 3, 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical significance from the flagella manipulation experiments.

claim: At 6 Hz, the compensation error was significantly different between the control and flagella-clipped groups in both twilight (p=0.0064) and dark conditions (p=0.0011).
source: At 6 Hz (Figure 3E), the compensation error was significantly different between the control (twilight: 0.7±0.02, dark: 0.7±0.05) and flagella-clipped (twilight: 0.8±0.03, dark: 1.0±0.03) groups in both twilight (p=0.0064) and dark conditions (p=0.0011) (Supplementary file 1c, 5, 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical significance from the flagella manipulation experiments.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory input is critical for head stabilization at 6 Hz.
source: These observations suggest that at 6 Hz, antennal mechanosensory input may be critical for head stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the flagella-clipping experiments showing impaired head stabilization at 6 Hz.

claim: After reattachment of flagella, the head stabilization was similar to the performance of the moths with intact antennae, for all conditions.
source: After reattachment of flagella, the head stabilization was similar to the performance of the moths with intact antennae, for all conditions.
evidence: This is a result from the flagella reattachment control experiments.

claim: For both 2 and 6 Hz rotations, the compensation error in flagella-reattached moths was not significantly different from the flagella-intact group under twilight and dark conditions.
source: For both 2 and 6 Hz rotations, the compensation error in flagella-reattached moths (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-L) was not significantly different from the flagella-intact group under twilight and dark conditions (see Supplementary file 1c, 3–6 for statistical comparisons).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the flagella reattachment experiments showing recovery of function.

claim: Antennal mechanosensory input is required for head stabilization in hawkmoths primarily at higher frequency, besides some contribution at lower frequency as well.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that antennal mechanosensory input is required for head stabilization in hawkmoths primarily at higher frequency, besides some contribution at lower frequency as well (Video 2).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the flagella manipulation experiments across frequencies.

claim: At 2 Hz in both twilight and dark conditions, the compensation error between the sham and Johnston's organ-glued groups was not significantly different.
source: Under twilight and dark conditions for 2 Hz roll stimulus, the compensation error between the sham (twilight: 0.4±0.02, dark: 1.2±0.08) and Johnston's organ-glued (JO-glued) groups (twilight: 0.4±0.01, dark: 1±0.04) was not significantly different (Figure 4E, p=0.5358, p=0.0831, Supplementary file 1c, 7, 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Johnston's organ gluing experiments.

claim: At 6 Hz in both twilight and dark conditions, the compensation error differed significantly between the sham and JO-glued groups.
source: At 6 Hz in both twilight and dark conditions, the compensation error differed significantly between the sham (twilight: 0.6±0.03, dark: 0.6±0.06) and JO-glued (twilight: 0.9±0.05, dark: 1±0.04) groups (Figure 4E, p=0.0097, p=0.0055, Supplementary file 1c, 9, 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical significance from the Johnston's organ gluing experiments.

claim: Feedback from the Johnston's organ affects head stabilization.
source: Thus, we observed similar effects in JO-glued and flagella-clipped moths (Figures 3A–B, E–4C–E), suggesting that feedback from the Johnston's organ affects head stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of effects between JO-glued and flagella-clipped moths.

claim: The flight duration of control (73±17.0 s) and sham (34±9.3 s) groups were significantly longer compared to the moths with restricted head-motion (1.5±0.7 s) (p=0.0001).
source: The flight duration of control (73±17.0 s) and sham (34±9.3 s) groups were significantly longer compared to the moths with restricted head-motion (1.5±0.7 s) (Figure 6A, p=0.0001, Supplementary file 1c, 11).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical significance from the free-flight experiments.

claim: The frequency of head-restricted moths colliding with the walls of flight chamber (1±0.1 per second) was significantly greater than in control (0.4±0.05 per second) and sham (0.3±0.05 per second) moths (p=0.0002).
source: The frequency of these moths (1±0.1 per second) colliding with the walls of flight chamber was significantly greater than in control (0.4±0.05 per second) and sham (0.3±0.05 per second) moths, thus indicating impairment in their flight performance (Figure 6B, p=0.0002, Supplementary file 1c, 12).
evidence: This is a quantitative result with statistical significance from the free-flight experiments.

claim: Head-restricted moths were unable to pitch up and stayed close to the ground usually touching it.
source: Whereas the control and sham moths took off smoothly and pitched up to a considerable height, the head-restricted moths were unable to pitch up, and consequently stayed close to the ground usually touching it, and became unstable as soon as they became airborne (Video 3).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the free-flight experiments.

claim: Compensatory head movements are crucial for stability in free-flight.
source: Compensatory head movements are crucial for stability in free-flight (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the free-flight experiments showing impaired flight in head-restricted moths.

claim: Compensatory head roll in tethered flight is mediated via a combination of visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback in the hawkmoth, D. nerii.
source: The data presented in this paper show that such compensatory head roll in tethered flight is mediated via a combination of visual and antennal mechanosensory feedback in the hawkmoth, D. nerii (Figure 5).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Despite the handicap of slow visual transduction rates, hawkmoths can fly or perform aerial maneuvers under low light levels.
source: Together, these studies show that despite the handicap of slow visual transduction rates, hawkmoths can fly or perform aerial maneuvers under low light levels.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from cited studies on hawkmoth vision.

claim: Gaze stabilization in D. nerii requires visual feedback at low temporal frequency, and antennal mechanosensory feedback at higher temporal frequencies.
source: Our data show that gaze stabilization in D. nerii requires visual feedback at low temporal frequency, and antennal mechanosensory feedback at higher temporal frequencies at which purely visual means of gaze stabilization may be constrained due to the requirement for both spatial and temporal pooling of photons to form images or derive motion information.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the experiments.

claim: Gaze stabilization is enhanced by a fast response via the antennal mechanosensory feedback loop which ensures that the head remains sufficiently stable to enable temporal and spatial integration of photons by the superposition eyes.
source: Specifically, we hypothesize that gaze stabilization is enhanced by a fast response via the antennal mechanosensory feedback loop which ensures that the head remains sufficiently stable to enable temporal and spatial integration of photons by the superposition eyes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental findings.

claim: Flagella-clipped moths were more strongly affected than the JO-glued moths, indicating some residual feedback from Johnston's organ after gluing the pedicel-flagellar joint.
source: In these experiments, flagella-clipped moths were more strongly affected than the JO-glued moths, indicating some residual feedback from Johnston's organ after gluing the pedicel-flagellar joint but not enough to ensure proper head stabilization (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of the two experimental manipulations.

claim: Flight impairment due to loss or reduction of Johnston's organ input may result in part from their inability to control compensatory head movements.
source: Thus, flight impairment due to loss or reduction of Johnston's organ input may result in part from their inability to control compensatory head movements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis connecting the head stabilization findings to previously observed flight impairments.

claim: In tethered hawkmoths, the gains for compensatory head movements ranged from 0.2 to 0.6 depending on the frequency of the forced body rotations under twilight condition.
source: In our experiments, the gains for compensatory head movements ranged from 0.2 to 0.6 depending on the frequency of the forced body rotations under twilight condition, which meant that the head was not fully stabilized in its horizontal orientation.
evidence: This is a summary of the gain values observed in the experiments.

claim: Head stabilization in tethered hawkmoths is undercompensated.
source: In our experiments, the gains for compensatory head movements ranged from 0.2 to 0.6 depending on the frequency of the forced body rotations under twilight condition, which meant that the head was not fully stabilized in its horizontal orientation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gain values being less than 1.

claim: Previous studies in diverse insects including flies, locusts, and wasps show that head stabilization does not fully compensate for the imposed stimulus.
source: Previous studies in diverse insects including flies (Hengstenberg et al., 1986), locusts (Hensler and Robert, 1990), and wasps (Viollet and Zeil, 2013) show that head stabilization does not fully compensate for the imposed stimulus.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Undercompensated head stabilization for low stimulus amplitudes has been previously observed in blowflies.
source: Undercompensated head stabilization for low stimulus amplitudes has also been previously observed in blowflies (Hengstenberg et al., 1986), suggesting that compensatory head rotations are only one of several components contributing to optomotor reflexes and are not the only mechanism involved in maintaining a level gaze.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and includes an inference about multiple mechanisms.

claim: Just as flies integrate haltere and visual feedback for head stabilization, the head stabilization reflex in moths also requires the integration of visual and antennal mechanosensory inputs.
source: A key result of these experiments is that, just as flies integrate haltere and visual feedback for head stabilization (Hardcastle and Krapp, 2016; Hengstenberg, 1993; Schwyn et al., 2011), the head stabilization reflex in moths also requires the integration of visual and antennal mechanosensory inputs.
evidence: This draws a parallel between the findings in moths and established knowledge about flies, supported by citations.

claim: Visual feedback influences head stabilization behavior in a lower frequency regime, whereas mechanosensory feedback influences head stability at a higher frequency regime.
source: A consistent result across these studies is that visual feedback influences head stabilization behavior in a lower frequency regime, whereas mechanosensory feedback – whether from antenna or halteres – influences head stability at a higher frequency regime.
evidence: This is a generalization drawn from the experimental results and comparison with other studies.

claim: In flies, halteres detect fast angular velocities of thorax rotation and elicit head stabilization with a gain of 0.1 around 50°/s, which reaches a maximum of about 0.75 at around 1000°/s.
source: In flies, halteres detect fast angular velocities of thorax rotation and elicit head stabilization with a gain of 0.1 around 50°/s, which reaches a maximum of about 0.75 at around 1000°/s (Hengstenberg, 1993; Sherman and Dickinson, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on fly halteres.

claim: In moths, antennal mechanosensory feedback affects tracking only at high frequencies (>2 Hz) of flower oscillations, whereas visual feedback is key at lower frequencies.
source: Similarly, in moths the antennal mechanosensory feedback affects tracking only at high frequencies (>2 Hz) of flower oscillations, whereas visual feedback is key at lower frequencies (Dahake et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dahake et al., 2018.

claim: In flies, some neck motor neurons require simultaneous activation of halteres and visual pathways for eliciting spikes, setting up a gating mechanism.
source: In flies, some neck motor neurons require simultaneous activation of halteres and visual pathways for eliciting spikes, thus setting up a gating mechanism which would enable compensatory head movements in a dynamic range that is in between the maximum sensitivities of the motion vision and haltere system (Huston and Krapp, 2009; Theobald et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on fly neck motor neurons.

claim: In the blowfly Calliphora vicinia, head wind and visual stimuli together elicit spikes in the ventral cervical nerve motorneuron (VCNM) of the neck motor system, but they do not individually fire action potentials in VCNM.
source: Whereas head wind and visual stimuli together elicit spikes in the ventral cervical nerve motorneuron (VCNM) of the neck motor system, they do not individually fire action potentials in VCNM in the blowfly, Calliphora vicinia.
evidence: This describes a specific finding about blowfly motor neurons.

claim: In the blowfly Calliphora vicinia, removal of the arista of the antenna abolished the VCNM response to combined head wind and visual stimuli.
source: In that study, the removal of the arista of the antenna abolished this VCNM response (Haag et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haag et al., 2010.

claim: Flies may possess a gating mechanism in the visual and antennal pathways that acts at the level of neck motor neurons.
source: Thus, flies may also possess a similar gating mechanism in the visual and antennal pathways that acts at the level of neck motor neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cited findings about blowfly motor neurons.

claim: It is likely that similar gating exists in the visual and antennal mechanosensory pathways in non-Dipteran insects.
source: It is likely that similar gating exists in the visual and antennal mechanosensory pathways in non-Dipteran insects.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to non-Dipteran insects.

claim: Small-amplitude head oscillations (or head wobble) at approximately 12 Hz were observed in all recordings of head stabilization.
source: In all the recordings of head stabilization, we observed small-amplitude head oscillations (or head wobble; Chatterjee et al., 2022) at approximately 12 Hz, which did not correspond to the wingbeat or any other frequency that we have investigated.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Regular head oscillations are a predicted outcome of the multisensory negative feedback loop and depend on the lag in sensory acquisition or its translation to motor commands.
source: These regular oscillations are a predicted outcome of the multisensory negative feedback loop that we have proposed, and depends on the lag in the sensory acquisition (Chatterjee et al., 2022), or its translation to motor commands in addition to the mechanical properties of head-neck apparatus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the origin of head wobble, supported by a citation.

claim: Head wobble may result from active head movements that the moth performs to ensure active visual feedback.
source: Alternatively, it may result from active head movements that the moth performs to ensure active visual feedback (Cellini and Mongeau, 2020; Stamper et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about head wobble, supported by citations.

claim: Head movements may help increase the dynamic range of the visual pattern movement speeds encoded by the insect motion-vision system.
source: Such head movements may help increase the dynamic range of the visual pattern movement speeds encoded by the insect motion-vision system (Windsor and Taylor, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Windsor and Taylor, 2017.

claim: Head stabilization in hawkmoths requires the combined feedback from the compound eyes and antennal mechanosensors.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that head stabilization in hawkmoths requires the combined feedback from the compound eyes and antennal mechanosensors.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: Under sufficient lighting and during slower turns, hawkmoths are able to stabilize their head using visual feedback.
source: Under sufficient lighting and during slower turns, hawkmoths are able to stabilize their head using visual feedback.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data at 2 Hz under twilight conditions.

claim: Under dark conditions or during faster turns, the role of antennal mechanosensory feedback from the Johnston's organs is essential for head stabilization.
source: However, under dark conditions or during faster turns, the role of antennal mechanosensory feedback from the Johnston's organs is also essential.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data at 6 Hz and under dark conditions.

claim: In absence of gaze stabilization, flight control in freely flying hawkmoths is severely impaired.
source: In absence of gaze stabilization, flight control in freely flying hawkmoths is severely impaired.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the free-flight experiments with head-restricted moths.

claim: The loss of flight control due to reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback may result at least partly from an inability to stabilize gaze.
source: Taken together, these results show that the loss of flight control due to reduction of antennal mechanosensory feedback may result at least partly from an inability to stabilize gaze.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings connecting antennal feedback, head stabilization, and flight control.

claim: For non-Dipteran insects such as hawkmoths, mechanosensory feedback is derived partly from the antennal Johnston's organs.
source: The data presented here show that for non-Dipteran insects such as hawkmoths, mechanosensory feedback is derived partly from the antennal Johnston's organs.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the Johnston's organ manipulation experiments.

claim: Adult D. nerii begin flying around sunset and remain active through the night at operating light levels of approximately 0.05–250 lux.
source: Adult D. nerii begin flying around sunset and remain active through the night (operating light levels: ~0.05–250 lux, unpublished observations).
evidence: This is an observation about the natural behavior of D. nerii.

claim: Moths were rotated at two frequencies: 2 Hz (low) and 6 Hz (high) for 8 cycles each, corresponding to mean angular speeds of 240°/s (low) and 720°/s (high), respectively.
source: We rotated the tether at two frequencies: 2 Hz (low) and 6 Hz (high) for 8 cycles each, corresponding to mean angular speeds of 240°/s (low) and 720°/s (high), respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The maximum stimulus frequency the stepper motor could reliably generate was 6 Hz.
source: The maximum stimulus frequency our stepper motor could reliably generate was 6 Hz.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the experimental setup.

claim: Frequencies of 2 Hz and 6 Hz are in alignment with the dynamic range of stimuli provided in previous studies of flower tracking in other hawkmoth species.
source: Frequencies of 2 Hz and 6 Hz are in alignment with the dynamic range of stimuli provided in previous studies of flower tracking in other hawkmoth species.
evidence: This justifies the choice of experimental frequencies based on previous studies.

claim: In the diurnal hawkmoth M. stellatarum, antennal mechanosensory feedback was reported to play a significant role in flower tracking in the frequency range of 2–5 Hz.
source: In the diurnal hawkmoth, M. stellatarum (Dahake et al., 2018), antennal mechanosensory feedback was reported to play a significant role in flower tracking in the frequency range of 2–5 Hz.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dahake et al., 2018.

claim: Under similar light levels used in this study, flower tracking was affected in the crepuscular hawkmoth M. sexta approximately in the frequency range of 2–8 Hz.
source: Further, under similar light levels used in our study, flower tracking was affected between the light levels in another study in the crepuscular hawkmoth, M. sexta, approximately in the frequency range of 2–8 Hz (Sponberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sponberg et al., 2015.
